summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, using SMIv2. It was a standards-track proposal. It was replaced by RFC 2358.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking Ethernet cards, written in a newer format. An even newer version replaced it.

subtitle: Management objects for Ethernet-like network interfaces using SNMPv2.

tldr.problem: Ethernet interfaces needed standardized management objects to monitor and diagnose performance and errors. Earlier definitions (RFC 1398) used SMIv1, and clearer guidance was needed on how interface MIBs relate to the evolving generic interface framework.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1650 defines the EtherLike-MIB module with tables for statistics (collisions, errors, transmissions), optional collision histograms, and two diagnostic tests: Time-Domain Reflectometry (TDR) for cable faults and loopback tests for chip diagnostics. All objects use SNMPv2 conventions and apply to Ethernet, ISO 8023, and StarLAN interface types.
tldr.outcome: It was superseded by RFC 2358, which further refined the definitions. This MIB remains the standard way to monitor Ethernet interface health and detect common problems like excessive collisions and carrier sense errors.

today: RFC 1650 was superseded by RFC 2358. The Ethernet MIB defined here remains the basis for all Ethernet interface management in SNMP-based network monitoring systems.

sections.title: Ethernet Interface Management
sections.content:
This RFC defines management objects for Ethernet-like network interfaces. It applies to three interface types: standard Ethernet (ifType 6), ISO 8023-CSMA/CD (ifType 7), and StarLAN (ifType 11). All three types share the same management characteristics and are treated identically by this MIB.

The definitions are based on the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management Specification and previous work in RFC 1284 and RFC 1398. The RFC updates earlier definitions to use SNMPv2 conventions and provides clarification on how Ethernet-like interfaces interact with the generic Interface MIB (RFC 1573).
sections.eli5: This is a standard way to see what is happening on Ethernet network cards using SNMP version 2.

sections.title: Statistics and Error Tracking
sections.content:
The dot3StatsTable tracks transmission and reception statistics for each Ethernet interface. Counters include alignment errors (frames with wrong length that fail checksum), FCS errors (frames of correct length that fail checksum), single and multiple collision frames (successful transmissions preceded by collisions), deferred transmissions (frames delayed while the medium was busy), late collisions (detected after 512 bit-times), excessive collisions (transmissions that fail), and internal MAC errors.

Receive-side errors include carrier sense errors (medium appeared busy when it was not, or vice versa), frame-too-long errors, and internal MAC receive errors. The table also identifies the Ethernet chip set being used, which helps correlate statistics to known hardware anomalies.
sections.eli5: A counter for each type of Ethernet transmission problem: collisions, errors, bad frames, and the chip type.

sections.title: Collision Histograms
sections.content:
The optional dot3CollTable provides a histogram of how many frames were transmitted after experiencing exactly N collisions, for N = 1 to 16. This histogram reveals the pattern of collisions on the segment: a normal Ethernet should see most transmissions succeed on the first try, with fewer collisions as the count increases. A segment with many frames experiencing 10+ collisions suggests congestion or a faulty interface.

Implementation of this histogram is optional, as not all Ethernet chips have the capability to track per-frame collision counts. However, it is valuable for troubleshooting and is recommended in systems with the necessary metering.
sections.eli5: A breakdown of how many times frames had to retry: how many made it on the first try, how many after one collision, after two, and so on.

sections.title: Diagnostic Tests
sections.content:
Two diagnostic tests are defined. The Time-Domain Reflectometry (TDR) test is a cable diagnostic that sends a pulse and measures the time until a collision or carrier deassertion is detected. The result, measured in 100-nanosecond units, can indicate the approximate distance to a cable fault. TDR is specific to traditional Ethernet and not applicable to 10BaseT (twisted pair) or 10BaseF (fiber). The test may need to be repeated to confirm a consistent result.

The loopback test is a full-duplex self-test that configures the MAC chip to loop transmitted data back internally, testing memory, data paths, and MAC logic. The interface must be offline for this test, and the chip must be reinitialized for network operation afterward.
sections.eli5: TDR measures the cable to find breaks. Loopback tests the network card chip itself by sending data around in a circle.

sections.title: Chipset Identification
sections.content:
Ethernet interfaces are built from multiple chips; the MIB identifies the Medium Access Control (MAC) chip using an OBJECT IDENTIFIER. Common chipsets are registered: AMD (7990, 79900, 79C940), Intel (82586, 82596), Seeq (8003), National (8390, Sonic), Fujitsu (86950), and Digital (DC21040). Identification allows network managers to correlate observed statistics to known limitations or bugs in specific chip revisions.

For chipsets not represented in the standard list, vendors are expected to assign OIDs in the enterprise subtree (RFC 1155).
sections.eli5: The MIB records which chip is in the network card. This helps explain any quirks in the statistics.
